claims.text: Wheat is central to the menu (ramen noodles, gyoza wrappers, soy-sauce-seasoned fried rice and stir-fries), so cross-contamination with gluten is effectively unavoidable in this kitchen.
Stir-fries and fried rice are seasoned with standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat; no gluten-free soy sauce is indicated.
Signature gyoza are pork-filled and most dishes use meat, egg, or seafood, with broths based on animal stock; vegan separation is not practiced.
Soba noodles here are not documented as pure buckwheat and are typically wheat-blended; tempura is fried in a shared kitchen, creating heavy gluten cross-contact.
Soba dipping broth (tsuyu) is soy-sauce and fish-dashi based; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat.
Broths are fish/bonito dashi based and the duck broth is explicitly dashi-seasoned; menu features duck, egg, and seafood tempura, so even soba dishes are not vegan.
Multilingual menus (English, Chinese, Korean) are available, making it easier for international diners to identify dishes.

name: 和風薬膳料理 紅茶 京小づち (Washoku Yakuzen Ryori Kocha Kyo Koduchi)

claims.text: Dishes are seasoned in the standard Japanese washoku style; regular soy sauce (which contains wheat) is the norm and no wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned.

Everything is cooked in katsuo (bonito) and kombu dashi, so even vegetable dishes are prepared in a fish-stock kitchen; the porridge uses chicken broth and the signature bento includes ancient cheese.
Menus describe each ingredient and its wellness effect, so diners can see what is in each component of the bento and course.
Heavy use of fresh seasonal Yamato vegetables and herbs means plenty of plant-forward components on the plate.

name: やまと庵 本店 (Yamato-an Honten)

claims.text: Menu is washoku-based with wheat-containing soy sauce, miso, tempura/fried items, and grilled Miwa somen (wheat noodles); no gluten-free accommodation is documented, so cross-contamination risk is high for celiacs.
Japanese soy sauce used throughout washoku menus is typically brewed with wheat; no wheat-free tamari is mentioned.
A meat-, game-, and fish-forward kitchen where fish dashi is used broadly; plant-based items would share preparation surfaces with animal products.
Some inherently lighter plant-based items appear on the menu, including local tofu, Yamato-vegetable dishes, a crisp daikon salad, and kuzu mochi.

name: ヤマトモダン JR奈良駅前店 (Yamato Modern JR Nara Ekimae-ten)

claims.text: Signature dishes use teriyaki/soy glazes (Yamato pork spare ribs) and breaded cutlets, indicating standard wheat-containing soy sauce and flour are in regular use.
The official site notes a 'healthy menu' can be requested, but no specific allergen, gluten-free or vegan handling protocol is documented.
A daily vegetable platter featuring Yamato vegetables and rice-flour pancakes are on the menu, giving some lighter or lower-wheat starting points to discuss with staff.

name: 大和薬食処 ならやま茶館 (Yamato Yakushokudokoro Narayama Sakan)

claims.text: Cuisine centers on tea porridge and Japanese home-style dishes that typically use wheat-containing soy sauce and miso; no gluten-free protocol is documented.
Traditional Yamato home cooking and tea porridge sides are normally seasoned with standard (wheat-based) soy sauce; gluten-free soy sauce is not mentioned.
The broth/dashi is made from natural ingredients from the sea (fish-based), and the kitchen uses fish, eggs, and dairy even on no-meat plates, so dishes are not vegan by default.
Guests complete a constitution/preference check sheet and the kitchen says it can prepare dishes tailored to a diner's preferences and symptoms, so dietary needs can be discussed when reserving.
Heavily vegetable-forward, using locally sourced seasonal organic Yamato vegetables prepared without chemical seasonings, with the option to adjust toward a meat-free plate on request.

name: やたがらす 奈良店 (Yatagarasu Nara-ten)

claims.text: Yakitori is glazed with wheat-containing tare and shares a charcoal grill; ponzu-dressed dishes also typically contain wheat-derived soy sauce. No gluten-free handling is documented.
Tare basting glaze and ponzu sauces used on signature dishes are soy-sauce based and normally contain wheat.
Kitchen is entirely chicken-centered; any vegetable dishes would be cooked alongside meat with fish/meat-based seasonings.

name: 萬御菓子誂處 樫舎 (Yorozu Onkashi Atsuraedokoro Kashiya)

claims.text: No gluten-free protocol is documented; the shop produces a range of traditional confections, some of which contain wheat, in a shared kitchen, so cross-contact with wheat cannot be ruled out.
No vegan handling is documented; the omakase course is chef's choice and some wagashi can contain egg or dairy, so vegans must confirm specific items in person.
Many core offerings are naturally plant-based (adzuki bean paste, glutinous rice, kinako, sugar) and tea service includes vegan matcha and Nara bancha.
